en: The *Ādikarmāvatāra* (Introduction to the Beginner’s Practice), composed by the learned elder Mañjukīrti.
Homage to the Buddha!
Homage to that Śrīghana, by whom, out of compassion for people, this boat of sequential stages was taught as the reality for crossing the great ocean of suffering. (1)
Indeed, in this world, the appearance of a Buddha is like the blooming of the udumbara flower; so too are hearing the Dharma taught by him and possessing faith.
Hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, barbarians, long-lived gods, those with wrong views, those born in the Buddha-less borderlands, and the mute—these are the eight inopportune states. (2)

Thus, being free from the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), the attainment of human existence is as difficult to obtain as a turtle’s neck entering the hole of a yoke floating upon the great ocean. Having realized that the convergence of all these factors is most exceedingly rare, one who possesses intense faith, skillful intelligence, and a mind encompassed by compassion should swiftly uproot—along with their very roots—the most terrifying sufferings of the miserable realms (*durgati*) arising from the sins accumulated in past and present lives. With the aim of attaining for oneself and leading others to the happiness of the fortunate realms (*sugati*) born of virtue and the perfections of the sons of the Sugata-Jinas, [one should strive] beyond transgression.

Preceded by the formal instruction, he practices according to the prescribed rule the going for refuge in the Three Jewels, the undertaking of the lay practitioner's vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), the generation of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), and its training. In that regard, this is the procedure for the confession of transgressions and so forth:

On an auspicious day, a pure son of noble family, having bathed and put on clean garments, should worship an image of the Tathāgata in a pleasing location. In front of that [image], he should prepare maṇḍalakas for the Three Jewels and for his teacher. Having first offered flowers and other gifts according to his means, he should prostrate before the Three Jewels. Then, having worshipped them to the best of his ability and given a fee, he should fall at the feet of his compassionate and learned teacher with a handful of flowers. Kneeling or squatting before him with palms joined, he should request three times as follows: "O spiritual friend, please grant me the three refuges preceded by the confession of sins, as well as the lay vows and the spirit of enlightenment. Then, observing that the disciple has been moved by sincere resolve, the teacher should say, preceded by an acceptance such as "I shall grant it to you according to my ability," "Speak, O long-lived one!"

May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me! May the Master attend to me! I, who am named so-and-so, whatever evil karma I have committed, caused others to commit, or rejoiced in, having encountered Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, my parents, or other sentient beings—whether in this life or in other future existences—all that, having gathered it together, condensed it, and weighed it, I confess with the foremost and most excellent confession in the presence of all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Master; acknowledging and remembering it, I do not conceal it.
Thus three times.

I, who am thus named, having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One—the Great Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, who has transcended all enmity and fear, the Great Man of indivisible and unsurpassed body, the Dharma-body, the foremost among two-legged beings.

I, who am thus named, having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Dharma—peaceful, the most excellent among those free from passion.

I, who am thus named, having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the irreversible community of Bodhisattvas, the best among assemblies. Thus three times.

Pay attention, O Teacher: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, have abstained from the taking of life; even so I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from the taking of life. By this first limb, I train myself in accordance with the training of those noble Arhats.

I shall practice and follow accordingly. Furthermore, just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, have abstained from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants; [so do I].

In the same way, I, [name], from this day forward for as long as life lasts, having abandoned taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, abstain from the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants. By this fifth limb, I train after the training of those noble ones, the Arhats; I follow it and imitate it. Thus a second time, thus a third time. It is appropriate and good.

I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, have gone for refuge to the Three Jewels and have received the *yāmaka* (watchful) vow for the sake of delivering, uplifting, and protecting the infinite realm of sentient beings from the sufferings of *saṃsāra*, and for establishing them in the unsurpassed knowledge of the Omniscient One. Just as those Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), have attained, are attaining, and will attain Buddhahood; and just as all Buddhas, through their unobstructed Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye, know and see, and having known the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, grant their approval—by that same method, I, [name], in the presence of the preceptor named [name] and before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, generate the thought of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. (This is repeated three times. Regarding this sequence beginning with the confession of transgressions followed by going for refuge to the Three Jewels: it is because pure qualities such as going for refuge cannot properly take root in a mind defiled by the stains of evil, just as white or red dyes cannot be applied to a garment that is extremely filthy. However, by means of this practice of remorse (*vidūṣaṇā-samudācāra*), the force of the flow of the defiled mind is checked; thereafter, when the continuum of the mind is inclined toward health and purity, going for refuge and other practices are much more easily able to arise.
Even most terrible deeds committed become diminished through self-reproach;
for they [are purified] by disclosure and by restraint.
"I declare that it is the complete uprooting of my very root," [as stated] in this saying.

By this, the practice of remorse (*vidūṣaṇā-samudācāra*) is expressed. And as for the practice of remorse: whatever unwholesome action one commits, one should feel a great abundance of regret for it very quickly and repeatedly. Furthermore, the benefits of going for refuge to the Three Jewels are explained in detail in the *Śūkarikā-avadāna*. For it is said: "Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth."
Having abandoned human bodies, they obtain divine bodies. ||4||

Thus, [it is said] regarding those who go for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and so forth. And in the *Triśaraṇānuśaṃsa-sūtra*: "In a single moment of thought, the merit arising from going for refuge is immeasurable;
it would surpass even the sky, were it possible for that sky to possess form. (5)
Therefore, if one desires the destruction of all substrates of existence, one should go for right refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, the supreme among assemblies. Thus it is said.

This should be understood extensively in this way from other sūtras as well. By this, the power of the basis (*āśrayabala*) is expressed; for even a powerful force that opposes evil is surely overcome by relying upon a powerful basis. From where does it follow that going for refuge (*śaraṇagamana*) precedes the formal undertaking of the vows (*saṃvara-samādāna*)? And what is the meaning of "refuge"? For going for refuge serves as the gateway to all formal undertakings of vows; therefore, it is prescribed first. As it has been said: "Mahānāman, when a householder, a man clothed in white, endowed with male faculties, goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma, and goes for refuge to the Saṅgha, and speaks these words: 'Hold me to be a lay follower (*upāsaka*) from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, until my breath ceases—toward all living beings, down to the smallest ant, possessing compassion for them,' and so forth. "Going for refuge to the Buddha" means one approaches the Blessed One, the Buddha—the teacher who points out the path to fearlessness—as a refuge, a protector, and a teacher. For one who has not accepted a teacher, his instruction lacks authority because of a lack of respect toward him. One goes for refuge to the Dharma, characterized by the ultimate pacification of all suffering, as the supreme goal and protection to be realized. Otherwise, how could one practice in order to directly realize it? One goes for refuge to the Saṅgha, which has become an invincible refuge and a state of fearlessness to be cultivated, through the attainment of serene confidence (*prasāda*) based on understanding. Thus...

Having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, he speaks these words: "Please consider me a lay follower (*upāsaka*). From this it is understood that going for refuge serves as the gateway for what precedes the formal undertaking of the vows. Thus, the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*) is the sense of protection; for by relying upon it, one is completely liberated from all suffering. As the Blessed One said:
"Many people, driven by fear, go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees. (Verse 7)
This refuge is not the best; this refuge is not the supreme.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering. (8)
But when one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha perceives the four noble truths with wisdom, [he becomes a true disciple]. (9)
Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the noble eightfold path leading to the security of Nirvana. ||10||
"This indeed is the best refuge; this is the supreme refuge.
Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.

(11) Thus, for one who has undertaken the observance of vows and so forth and who seeks refuge even while upholding the Teacher’s instruction in the world, he prescribes these training rules (*śikṣāpada*). "Then I accept you. If you do not dwell with them for even a moment—though they appear through the body as various things that are sweet at first encounter but bitter in their ultimate transformation, and though they are perceived as such by you—"

You maintain association with Devadatta and others who are harmful at first sight; yet you never transgress my word—why is that? Because one is protected by not violating his command, and not otherwise. Now, regarding this person who undertakes the five-limbed vow of lay discipline (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), does he refrain from all ten unwholesome paths of action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), or only from some of them? If it were only from some, then his possession of the ten wholesome paths of action would not be established. If, on the other hand, he refrains from all of them, then it must be explained how this is so. For the three types of misconduct (*duścarita*) of body, speech, and mind are taught respectively as three, four, and three of the ten unwholesome paths of action, taken collectively. And this person, while undertaking the vow of abstinence, takes up restraint only from the threefold misconduct of the body and from the single [misconduct] of speech, namely false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), but not from the others. How then could there be for him the possession of the ten wholesome paths of action? He who refrains from false speech must also avoid the other faults of speech known as slander (*paiśunya*), harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), and frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).

In this way, one becomes endowed with good verbal conduct (*vāksucarita*). If this is so, why is it said that there is abstention from false speech alone, and not from all forms of verbal misconduct (*vāgduścarita*), as is the case with bodily misconduct (*kāyaduścarita*) and the rest, which are taught separately and in their entirety? For while all three types of bodily misconduct are individually and exclusively censured in the world—because they involve the taking of life and the infliction of injury, and are therefore utterly condemned—it is not the same for verbal misconducts. Among these, only false speech is utterly censured. Therefore, in the instruction on the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the Lords of Sages have prescribed abstention from false speech alone. This is by way of introduction: false speech is indeed utterly censured and more gross than the others; thus, one who has abstained from it has entered the path of good verbal conduct, and [the teacher] himself encourages such a person to abstain from those other [verbal faults]. However, what is truly intended is abstention from all of them.

As it has been said: "In this case, monks, a son of good family or a daughter of good family is endowed with faith. Though he may be prone to negligence, he has faith in and accepts the ripening of all karma; he is free from doubt. Having understood that there is no loss of the fruit of black and white karmas, he does not commit what ought not to be done even for the sake of his life. He abstains from taking life. He abstains from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, from malicious speech, from harsh speech, from frivolous chatter, from covetousness, from ill-will, and from wrong view. Having undertaken these ten paths of wholesome action, he conducts himself accordingly and does not resort to the ten unwholesome paths of action," and so forth.

Therefore, one who abstains from false speech should also avoid malicious speech and the others. What benefit is gained by this? In this way, he becomes one whose actions are purified, because he is well-restrained in both body and speech. Let it be so regarding the abstention from misconduct of body and speech; but how is there abstention from misconduct of mind? Because this very abstention from misconduct of body and speech is originated precisely by the three wholesome roots—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—through wholesome mental states. Therefore, the cessation of covetousness and the rest is established as non-covetousness, non-malice, and right view. This is because covetousness, malice, and wrong view have greed, hatred, and delusion as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The meaning is that when non-greed and the others exist, non-covetousness and the others are established. In this manner, all ten wholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*) are included. Furthermore, what benefit is obtained through the possession (*samanvāgama*) of these? These ten wholesome paths of action are the cause of prosperity and liberation. There are three types of prosperity: prosperity of the physical basis (*ātmabhāva*), prosperity of enjoyments (*bhoga*), and prosperity of external things.

These serve as the causes for all three types of excellence (*sampatti*); that is to say, they bring about the three fruits: the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). There are also three liberations (*vimukti*) according to the distinction of the three vehicles; this, moreover, is the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*). In this regard, these [ten wholesome paths of action] function as causes through a continuous succession. As it has been said: “O Lord of Serpents, just as all villages, towns, market towns, kingdoms, and capitals; all medicinal herbs, grasses, shrubs, and trees; all occupations; and the entire multitude of seeds and the crops that are sown and grow—depend upon the earth as their foundation; even so, O Lord of Serpents, these very ten wholesome paths of action are the foundation for rebirth among gods and humans, the basis for the attainment of the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*), for individual enlightenment (*pratyekabodhi*), for the conduct of all bodhisattvas, and indeed for all the qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, the other ten unwholesome paths of action are the cause of all misfortune (*vipatti*). They must be avoided by those who desire prosperity, let alone by those who desire liberation. All misfortunes consist of the misfortune of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), the misfortune of enjoyments (*bhoga*), and the misfortune of external things (*bāhyabhāva*). As it has been said: “Monks, by fully practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing all ten unwholesome paths of action to an excessive degree, one is reborn in the hells; by a middling degree, in the animal realm; and by a mild degree, one is reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). This is their fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).”

"When he thus comes to the common lot of human beings, through the taking of life he becomes short-lived; through taking what is not given, he suffers the loss of wealth; through sexual misconduct, his wife has rivals; through false speech, he is frequently slandered; through malicious speech, there is a division among his friends; through harsh speech, he hears unpleasant sounds; through idle chatter, his words are not accepted; through covetousness, he has intense passion; through malice, he has intense hatred; and through wrong view, he has intense delusion. This is their result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*)."

"Through the taking of life, external things become weak in vitality (*alpa-ojas*). Through taking what is not given, they abound in dust and dirt. Through sexual misconduct, they are strewn with dust. Through false speech, they are foul-smelling. Through divisive speech, they are uneven—having highs and lows. Through harsh speech, they are saline, arid, and desolate wastelands, wretched and evil lands. Through idle chatter, they have irregular seasonal transformations. Through covetousness, their fruits are meager. Through malice, their fruits are bitter. Through wrong view, they have little fruit or no fruit at all; this is their dominant result (*adhipati-phala*). For by one who commits the taking of life, suffering is produced for others, their life is cut off, and their vitality is destroyed."

From causing suffering, one is reborn among the wicked; from the cutting off of life, one has a short lifespan among humans, such that one dies prematurely; from destroying vitality, external things become lacking in vigor. This should be applied similarly to taking what is not given and the other [non-virtuous paths]. Thus, by practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing all ten wholesome paths of action, one is reborn among the gods; this is their fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*).

If he comes here to the common lot of human beings, by abstaining from taking life he becomes long-lived; by abstaining from taking what is not given he possesses great wealth from others; and so on, up to: by abstaining from wrong view he has little delusion—this is their outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*).

For by one who practices abstention from taking life, happiness is produced for others through the gift of fearlessness, assistance is rendered by preserving their lives, and vitality is protected; thus, this fruit is threefold. This same principle should be applied to the other [precepts] as well. By this much, the power of restoration (*pratyāpatti-bala*) has been explained. Through the undertaking of the equipment of ethical discipline (*śīla-sambhāra*), one attains the restraint of non-action; this is the power of restoration.

The benefits of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) are described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūhasūtra*: "O son of good family, the thought of awakening is indeed the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha; it is the field, because it causes the growth of the pure qualities of the entire world; it is the earth, because it is the refuge for all the world; it is the father, because it protects all bodhisattvas; it is Vaiśravaṇa, because it cuts through all poverty; it is the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), because it accomplishes all aims; it is the auspicious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*), because it fulfills all intentions; it is the spear, because it conquers the enemy of the afflictions (*kleśa*)," and so forth, in detail.

Thus, the bodhicitta, which possesses such benefits, is of two kinds: first, the mind of aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhipraṇidhicitta*); and second, the mind of application toward enlightenment (*bodhiprasthānacitta*). The mind that aspires toward enlightenment, or the mind directed toward it—which arises from the vow and is devoid of the actual engagement in giving and so forth—is the *praṇidhicitta*. For example, it is the initial volition in the form of a prayer, as previously stated: "May I become a Buddha for the sake of protecting all living beings. The mind of application, or the application itself as the mind—because the mind has that very nature—is that which, preceded by the aforementioned mental attention, begins from the moment one undertakes the vows and engages in the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*).

"...that mind of setting forth proceeds. This twofold [mind] is indeed the *bodhicitta* itself, because even the *bodhicitta* generated through deceit is stated to be a cause for Buddhahood in the *Śūraṅgamasūtra*. Likewise, it is said in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*: "O son of good family, rare are those beings in the world of beings who direct their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; rarer still than they are those beings who have actually set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By this, the state of not relinquishing the *bodhicitta* is expressed. And by all of this, it is stated that through the application of the aforementioned practices such as the non-practice of faults, a practitioner overcomes even the evil that has been committed and accumulated. As it is said in the *Caturdharmakasūtra*:
Having committed even a slight evil, the fool sinks downward;
having performed even great deeds, the wise man abandons all misfortunes.
For even a small amount of compacted matter sinks in water.
"Even that which is great floats when it has been placed in a vessel.

Thus it was said by the venerable Vasubandhu in his commentary on the phrase "purifying the power of karma": "In that regard, the 'power' of unwholesome karma that is certain to be experienced is its capacity to yield the fruit of the three miserable destinies. Purifying that—meaning removing or vomiting it out—by means of the power of remorse and so forth, as it is said: 'I have committed most terrible deeds...'"
They become attenuated through self-reproach;
by means of their disclosure and restraint, I declare their ultimate uprooting. (13)

And by purifying [the mind] through the power of the antidote (*pratipakṣabala*), just as in the case of Maitreya-kalpaka: although an unwholesome karma arising from insulting his mother was set to yield its ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) in this very life due to the excellence of the field (*kṣetra*), and although some of it had already been given, that karma was entirely and utterly eradicated and destroyed simply by the arising of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicittotpāda*) born of a specific intention to benefit beings. What is this "arising of the resolve for enlightenment directed toward the welfare of beings"? It is said: "Whatever beings there may be in the entire world who will commit such unwholesome karma arising from insulting their mothers, just as I have done—for the sake of all of them, I alone shall experience, continuously and until the end of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), a single mass of infinite great suffering produced by the crushing of wheels upon my head; may not even a single being ever come here [to suffer]. Also, by the power of the basis (*āśrayabala*): as in the *Śūkarikā-avadāna*, a certain son of the gods subject to death was reborn in the womb of a sow in a pit, with karma ready to yield its fruit; yet, merely by going for refuge to the Three Jewels, he completely uprooted it all, and passing away from the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*), was reborn among the Tuṣita gods. Furthermore, through the penetration of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*), there occurs an internal extraction [of the defilements].

As it is said in the *Karmāvaraṇapratiprasrabdhi-sūtra*: "For example, a certain monk was charged with two grains of mustard seed for the offenses of unchastity and the killing of a human being. Later, his mind became agitated and his heart was filled with remorse; like one driven mad, he wandered from monastery to monastery and from village to village, even entering the streets. Proclaiming that evil deed before all people, crying out again and again, 'I am robbed! I am robbed! and making a sound of lamentation, he thinned out that karma by means of vomiting it up through the power of confessing his transgression. For the sake of that very person whose mind was thus tormented, a certain Bodhisattva who had attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) taught the Dharma in such a way that it was profound, whereby he uprooted that evil entirely and, through the penetration of the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*), became an attainer of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). One should have faith that this resolute conviction in the profound Dharma dispels all remorse regarding downfalls and purifies all karmic obscurations.

As it is taught in the *Āryatathāgatakośasūtra*: "Kāśyapa, if one were to deprive of life one who is both a father and a pratyekabuddha, this is the foremost of acts of taking life. This is the foremost of acts of taking what is not given: namely, the theft of the Three Jewels. This is the foremost of sexual misconducts: namely, if one were to cause a woman who is both one’s mother and a nun to burn. This is the foremost of false speech: namely, slandering the Tathāgata. This is the foremost of divisive speech: namely, causing a schism in the Saṃgha. This is the foremost of harsh speech: namely, reviling the noble ones. This is the foremost of idle chatter: namely, distracting those who desire the Dharma. This is the foremost of covetousness: namely, [coveting] those who have attained the right path."
The intent to steal for the sake of obtaining wisdom is the foremost among malicious thoughts; namely, the attempt at an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) is the foremost.

[This refers to] those with wrong views, namely, those whose views are extremely dense. These ten unwholesome paths of action are all greatly blameworthy. Kāśyapa, if some single being were to be possessed of these ten unwholesome paths of action that are so greatly blameworthy, yet were to enter into the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma associated with causes and conditions—realizing that herein there is no self, no being, no life-principle, and no person who acts or who experiences [the result]—and thus enters into the fact that all phenomena are uncreated, unconditioned, undefiled, illusory by nature, and luminous by essence; and if he has faith in and is resolved upon all phenomena as being primordially pure, I do not say that such a being goes to a state of sin."

For what reason? There is no accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*). All afflictions arise, break, and dissolve; they arise through the conjunction of a collection of causes and conditions, and as soon as they have arisen, they cease. O Blessed One, that which is the breaking of the arising of the mind is itself the breaking of all afflictions. For one who has such conviction, there is never any transgression (*āpatti*), nor any occasion for transgression. It is impossible—that is, there is no room for it—that one should abide in a transgression within the unobstructed state; such a thing cannot exist. Thus, by the very manifestation of the arousal of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), there occurs the absolute eradication of all unwholesome states originating from transgressions.

As it is said in the *Upāliparipṛcchā Sūtra*: "If a bodhisattva should incur an offense in the forenoon, but brings the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to mind at midday, that aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of that bodhisattva should be known as unimpaired. Likewise, if he should incur an offense at midday, but brings the thought of awakening to mind in the afternoon, that aggregate of ethical discipline of that bodhisattva should be known as unimpaired—and so on."

And so it is said in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha-sūtra*: "Noble son, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is like the fire at the end of an eon, because it incinerates all misdeeds," and so forth. Also, in the *Triśatikā*, it says: "Subhūti, those sons of good family or daughters of good family who shall take up, preserve, recite, and master such sūtras as these—they will be despised, they will be thoroughly despised. Why is that? Because whatever impure karmas those beings committed in previous lives which would have led to rebirth in the miserable states, those [karmas] will be exhausted through being despised in this very life."

By such means as these, the complete purification of non-virtuous karma that is certain to be experienced is accomplished. As for those who say: "Let it be granted that mild or middling non-virtuous karma may be entirely uprooted through the power of confession and so forth; but how can there be a total and absolute uprooting of the roots of heavy karma, such as the *ānantarya* [immediate] sins?"—to this it is replied: In the case of Ajātaśatru and others who committed the *ānantarya* sins, there were distinctions of mild, middling, and intense intention by which they would have had to remain in the Avīci hell for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*), or for half of one, or even less. For their sake, because their minds were scorched by the fire of remorse and they were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*samvega*), that karma was diminished through the power of confession and so forth. Since it is taught that the fruit of that karma was to be experienced at a time as brief as the falling of a ball, does this not mean, in effect, that there was a total uprooting of the roots of that karma? Indeed, a field is not left unharvested simply because a single stalk remains uncut. Furthermore, how is the exhaustion of such a vast heap of karma achieved? It is not like what remains when only a fly's footprint is left behind. For even in that case, if the engagement of the remedial volition (*pratipakṣacetanā*) had been performed, it certainly would have reached exhaustion.
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having reached the convergence of conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. (14)

How is such a passage to be interpreted? This confession is to be understood as applying to those actions which have not been suppressed or attenuated by the power of practices such as remorse (*vidūṣaṇā*). And so it has been said: "The fool, having committed even a small evil, goes downward;
the wise man, having committed even a great one, abandons all misfortunes."
This [clay] sinks even in a small amount of water when it is compacted, yet that very same substance floats when fashioned into a vessel, however large. Thus [it is said]. (15)

Thus, by one who has performed the going for refuge, obtained the lay vows (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), and undertaken the practice for awakening—though lacking great faith and possessing only modest wisdom—who has taken refuge at the feet of the Guru and is a seeker of the welfare of beings, the preliminary practices (*ādikarma*) such as the construction of a *caitya*, the striking of all [instruments], the offering of water to Jambhala, the offering of water-oblations (*bali*) to the *preta*s, and the propitiation of the Perfect Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, should be practiced according to the rules. For the attainment of the unsurpassed fruit is preceded by those [practices]. Now, as to how many these preliminary practices are, he says:
The five perfections are taught under the designation of "initial action," yet their intrinsic nature does not exceed that of the perfection of wisdom. (16)
Now, what is the fruit of these? He says:
Giving and ethical discipline are the causes for the Enjoyment Body;
meditation and wisdom are the causes for the Dharma Body; while vigor is considered the cause for both. (17)

In that regard, first is the procedure for constructing a caitya: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vairocanaprabharāja, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. It is as follows: Oṃ, O subtle one, O subtle one, O equal one, O moment, O peaceful one, O tamed one, O established one, O supportless one, O Taraṃba, O Yaśovatī, O you of great splendor, O unconfused one, O Nirvāṇa, empowered by the empowerment of all Buddhas, svāhā!

Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over a lump of clay or a lump of sand, one should fashion a caitya. As many atoms as there are in it, so many tens of millions of caityas are thereby made. One obtains merits equal in number to those atoms and becomes a lord of the ten stages (daśabhūmīśvara). One will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vairocana:
"Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause."
And that which is the cessation of these—such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. ||18||

Having established oneself with this verse: *Oṃ namo bhagavate puṣpaketurājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya | tadyathā—oṃ puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpodbhave puṣpasaṃbhave puṣpāvakīrṇe svāhā* | one should offer a flower after consecrating it seven times with this dhāraṇī.

"As many flowers as there are, so many tens of millions of flowers are offered. Then, one should perform the veneration of the *caitya* with this dhāraṇī: "Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Perfectly Awakened One, Ratnaketurāja. It is thus: Oṃ ratne ratne mahāratne ratnavijaye svāhā. By performing this single veneration of the *caitya*, ten million venerations of *caityas* are accomplished. This is the ritual procedure for constructing a *caitya*.
Now, according to the *Mahāmaṇḍalavyūha-tantra*, the ritual procedure for all types of striking is set forth. Homage to all Buddhas! Oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā. This is the mantra for taking the clay.
Or: Oṃ vasudhe svāhā.
Oṃ vajradbhavāya svāhā—this is the mantra for bowing to the image.
Oṃ araje viraje svāhā—this is the mantra for anointing with oil.
Oṃ vajradhātugarbhe svāhā—this is the mantra for placing the image [in the mandala].
Oṃ dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā—this is the mantra for casting the clay.
Oṃ vajramudgara ākoṭaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—this is the mantra for striking.
Oṃ dharmarate svāhā—this is the mantra for drawing out the clay.
Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajre svāhā—this is the mantra for installation.
Oṃ sarvatathāgatamaṇiśatadīpte jvala 2 dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā—this is the mantra for consecration. Oṃ svabhāva-viśuddhe āhara 2 āgaccha 2 dharmadhātugarbhe svāhā—this is the mantra for dismissal.
Oṃ ākāśadhātugarbhe svāhā—this is the mantra for requesting forgiveness. Thus concludes the procedure for all acts of striking.

Thereafter: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām apratihatashāsanānām oṃ kiṇi 2 tathāgatodbhavaśānte varade uttamottamatathāgatodbhave hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. By the retention of this, the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra* becomes retained. *Namo bhagavatyai āryaprajñāpāramitāyai*. It is as follows: *Oṃ munidharme saṃgrahadharme anugrahadharme vimuktidharme sadānugrahadharme vaiśravaṇaparivarttitadharme sarvakāryapariprāpaṇadharme samatānuparivarttitadharme svāhā*. *Oṃ prajñe śrutismṛtivijaye dhī dhāraṇīye svāhā*. By the retention of this, the *Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* becomes retained. *Namaḥ samanta-*

*Oṃ dhuna dhuna hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!* By the retention of this, the *Ārya-samādhirāja-sūtra* is retained. *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāmapratihataśāsanānām oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!* By the retention of this, the *Mahāpratisarā* is retained. Having paid homage to these *dhāraṇīs*, beginning with the single verse, and to the noble ones, one should install them and that reliquary (*caitya*) and so forth in an undisturbed location.
And the benefits of these two are as follows:
As many atoms as there are in the stupas or images of the Blessed One, so many kingdoms shall certainly belong to its maker, both in heaven and on earth. (19)

Having enjoyed all the happiness resulting from the perfection of the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms without exception, one finally attains the state of a Buddha, which is free from birth, old age, and misfortune. (20)
And from the *Prasenajitparipṛcchā*:

"Those who have an image of the Jina made here in this world become endowed with beauty, good fortune, and virtuous qualities; their senses are guarded, they possess the brilliance of the sun, and they become delightful to the eyes of the world. (21)
The body of one who fashions a Sugata’s body—tender, magnificent, and seated upon a lotus—becomes perfectly pure, liberated from disease, grief, fear, and suffering. (22)

Those who have a statue of the Jina made here do not go into servitude, nor into a state of poverty, nor into the condition of being a messenger, nor even into a low birth; nor do they suffer any deficiency of the sense faculties. (23)

Those people who worship the image of the Sage with noble garlands and showers of excellent flowers become, in the worlds of gods and humans, beautifully adorned and possessed of wondrous, pleasing complexions. (24)

With their grief destroyed, their limbs made firm, and having become preeminent with vast treasuries of jewels, those who have conquered the hosts of their enemies will indeed become wise by causing the preparation of this rice-pudding for the Lord of Munis. (25)
Now the instruction for the gift of the water-jar (jambhala-kalaśa) is set forth:
[The practitioner], seated upon a moon-mandala purified by the syllable *ka*, together with the fluids of Śāśvata and the others arising from the five seed-syllables beginning with *dhūṃ*. (26)
One should offer water mixed [with the mantra], withdrawing the index finger, while visualizing Jambhala before oneself and the syllable *JAM* upon his head. (27)
Having stepped upon the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, who are seated on his wings, he wears a crown of vajras and the sun, is yellow in color, and wears a garland of blue lotuses. ||28||
Holding a *kārañja*, a *nakulī*, and a *bījapūraka* fruit, [he should offer] that which has been consecrated with the mantra:
*oṃ jambhalajaledrāya svāhā*. (29)

The Ritual for Offering Water and Food to Jambhala: Reciting "Oṃ, this water for all pretas, svāhā," one should offer water to all pretas while maintaining a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Then, recite: "Homage to the Tathāgata Surūpa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. That is to say: Oṃ suru suru, prasuru prasuru, bhara bhara, sambhara sambhara, smara smara, [this is] for all pretas, svāhā. Having consecrated food together with water seven times with this *dhāraṇī*, and having snapped the fingers three times with the left hand, it should be offered to all pretas in a secluded place.

And it should be spoken thus: "May those who look for an opportunity to harm depart! I give food to all the *preta*s dwelling in all the world-systems. This must be performed while one has not yet eaten. In this way, a meal of one *droṇa* of rice is given to each and every *preta*. By acting in this manner, one does not become weak; one does not become poor. On the contrary, in birth after birth, one becomes very powerful, handsome, beautiful to behold, wealthy, and possessed of great enjoyments. One will have a long life and be a practitioner of yoga, and will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Having passed away, one is reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī. This is the *dhāraṇī* named Surūpā.
Homage to all Buddhas! O you who behold all Tathāgatas! Oṃ bhara bhara sambhara sambhara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

Having recited this mantra seven times, one should visualize the doors [of the city] filled by streams of nectar issuing from the five fingers of the outstretched right hand; then, having sprinkled the ground with water mixed with the remains of the bali offering, one should see the food being served in Magadhan droṇas. While satiating the entire host of pretas, one should snap the fingers three times and offer the bodhisattva bali. This is the ritual for the water-offering to pretas and so forth.
But he who is supreme in worshiping the Buddha is not overcome by the Māras. ||30||

Thus, according to the teaching, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles, one should worship all the Buddhas according to the ritual in mandalas that are semicircular, triangular, circular, or square—corresponding to the purity of the four continents of Pūrvavideha, Jambudvīpa, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru—or else in whichever mandala is desired among these. In this regard, the ritual is as follows:

"At the end of the night, remaining in bed and well-composed, one should practice meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the recitation of mantras until liberation; then, while still on the bed, one should perform the recollection (*anusmṛti*) of the Buddha and the others. (31)

Then, having performed the cleansing of the mouth, bathing, and the washing of the hands and other limbs, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the appropriate mantras, both externally and internally, for the satisfaction of one's own self.

In this regard, the mantra for bathing is: *oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ hūṃ*. This same bathing mantra applies even to images and the like. *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ* is the mantra for the protection of the site, oneself, and the yoga. *Oṃ hrīḥ svāhā* is the mantra for washing the hands and sipping water. *Oṃ hūṃ* is the mantra for the consecration of the seat. This procedure also applies at the time of constructing a *caitya* and so forth. Having sprinkled the ground with the mantra for purifying the earth, *oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ svāhā*, one recites: *oṃ vajrabhūme hūṃ*.

With this, one should perform the appropriation of the site (*bhūmiparigraha*). Having taken cow dung and other materials with water using the mantra *oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ svāhā*, one should begin the mandala on a clean area of ground. *Oṃ āḥ vajrarekhe hūṃ* is the mantra for the mandala.
At the time of sweeping, one should recite the praise of the mandala, beginning with: "The gift is cow dung," and so forth.

Then, once the sweeping is completed, one should recite: *Oṃ surekhe sarvatathāgatā adhitiṣṭhantu svāhā*. Having spoken thus, taking a single flower with the left hand, placing it upon the back of the right hand, and dropping it into the maṇḍala, one should wash the hands. Then, while scattering the flower upon one’s own head, one should perform self-protection with the mantra: *Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare rakṣa 2 māṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. From the making of the maṇḍala, there is the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), as well as qualities such as a golden radiance and so forth. For it is said in the *Maṇḍalānuśaṃsā*:
Charity is cow-dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is thorough sweeping; patience is the removal of ants and termites; vigor is the exertion of effort;
meditation is making the mind one-pointed for that moment; and wisdom is the bright, beautiful lines [of the mandala].
Having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections. //33//
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases, distinguished among gods and men, with a radiant splendor like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
"Having performed bodily actions in this supreme abode of the Sugata.

(34) Thus, having thus brought forth the maṇḍala and having perceived that maṇḍala in the form of a rising dawn-colored moon-disc and so forth, one should empower it with the mantra: *oṃ candrārkavimale svāhā*.
Then, one should meditate upon a mountain endowed with continents in the center of that maṇḍala.
Having performed the placement of the Goddess and the Victor, one should then worship her mantra. ||35||
There, in Pūrvavideha, is the white Sage Vairocana;
he is born from the seed-syllable Oṃ and is joined with the Bodhyaṅgī mudrā. ||36||
Ratnasambhava, the bestower of boons, is yellow, has the seed-syllable TRĀṂ, and resides on Jambūdvīpa;
Amitābha, the Victor, is red, has the seed-syllable HRĪḤ, and dwells in Godānīya absorbed in meditative concentration. ||37||
Amoghasiddhi is green, with the gesture of granting fearlessness, and has the seed-syllable Khaṃ; he resides in Kuru.
Akṣobhya is blue, born from the syllable Hūṃ, stands upon Mount Sumeru, and is marked by the earth-touching mudrā. ||38||
Here, Vairocana is situated upon the moon, while the remaining [deities] are established upon the sun;
they possess the five wisdoms and the nature of the three bodies, wear the uṣṇīṣa, and are adorned with robes. (39)
All the goddesses seated upon lotuses are situated in the corner regions.
In the southeast is Locanā, white in color, born from the syllable LĀṂ, holding a wheel, and steadfast. (40)
In the southwest is Māmakī, blue, born from *māṃ*, swift, and endowed with a vajra;
in the northwest is Pāṇḍarā, red, born from *pāṃ*, warm, and possessing a red lotus. (41)
In the northeast is Tāriṇī, dark green in color, born from the syllable Tāṃ, seated upon a blue lotus;
she is the goddess Vajradhātvīśvarī, who abides everywhere and at all times. (42)
Therefore, its description here has not been shown separately;
rather, it is within that orb of the sun produced from the syllable *A*. (43)
Yaṃ—there should be a multicolored eight-petaled lotus;
as before, by means of the seed-syllables situated upon it, the maṇḍala is emanated as a lamp. (44)
One should worship the entire mandala, which consists of the three principles (tritattva), according to the prescribed ritual.
Having drawn forth the Jñānasattva by means of the sequence *jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ*, the devoted person should attract, cause to enter, bind, and satisfy it. (45)
Alternatively, one should invoke [the deities] preceded by the individual recitation of their names: *Oṃ āgaccha 2 bhagavann akṣobhya vajra āḥ*.

Having performed the external worship with flowers and so forth, one should perform the mental worship. Having performed the offering of the mandala and other rites, one should respectfully perform the hymns of praise and so on. (46)
In that regard, one should first offer flowers to the Lord of the Mandala with the three-syllable mantra;
afterwards, one should present them to all [the deities] with their respective individual mantras. ||47||
Having first uttered "Oṃ Vajraṃ," and placing "Puṣpe" and so forth in the middle, one should offer [the oblation] to the deities with the mantra ending in "Āḥ Hūṃ Svāhā. (48)

Alternatively, according to this sequence, one should offer [the flowers] three times for each: Oṃ namo 'kṣobhyāya hūṃ | Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo vairocanāya oṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svā | Oṃ namo ratnasambhavāya trāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo 'mitābhāya hrīḥ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo 'moghasiddhaye khaṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo locanāyai lāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namo māmakye māṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namaḥ pāṇḍarāyai pāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ namas tārāyai tāṃ oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ svāhā | Furthermore, one should offer a great abundance of flowers to Akṣobhya. Following this same sequence, one should present the five offerings with: Oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajradīpe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajragandhe hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ vajranaivedye hūṃ svāhā | Thus, one should present the five types of offerings.

In that regard, for Vairocana it is the form of lamps and so forth; for Ratnasambhava, the scent of sandalwood and so forth; for Amitābha, the taste of milk and so forth; for Amoghasiddhi, the tangible objects such as clothing; and for Akṣobhya, the pleasant sounds of lutes and so forth. Thus, having properly presented these five sensory qualities as their primary offerings:

“Oṃ, radiate this *gaganaka* [offering] from the mass of spreading clouds of offerings to all Tathāgatas, Hūṃ!”—thus one should consecrate the offering. If one is unable [to perform physical offerings], one should perform a great mental offering as well. For example: various types of garments, banners, jewels, pearls, necklaces, and so forth; various types of flowers such as the *padma* and *utpala*; various types of requisites such as waist-bands, alms bowls, robes, and water-strainers; and the four continents and sub-continents filled with the seven precious gems and other riches—all these should be offered through the power of the Buddha’s blessings and by the force of mantra and *vidyā*.
In the assembly of the Perfectly Awakened One, born from my own vow. ||49||
May clouds of offerings, established in universal auspiciousness, proceed from every direction;
having reflected thus with effort and with a perfectly steady mind. (50)

Then, one should recite this Great Queen of Spells (*mahāvidyārājñī*), which effects the accomplishment of worship, eight times: *namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvathodgate sphurahi (sphurihi) imaṃ gaganakaṃ samantataḥ svāhā*. Thereupon, clouds of unfailing offerings, as they have been manifested, abide for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are worthy of worship. However, in the case of worship directed toward an image, one should perform the bathing with: *oṃ āḥ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ hūṃ*, and then perform the offerings and so forth as previously described.

Then, I, [name], offer myself in every way and at all times to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, together with their retinues, who have entered the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). May those Great Compassionate Ones empower me and protect me; may they grant me accomplishment and the supreme boon. This is the offering of oneself.

Thereafter, I confess all sins born of attachment, aversion, and delusion, committed at all times. I confess with those very mental states that have been taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—just as those Blessed Buddhas know them. This is the confession of sins.

Then, one should perform the rejoicing in merit (*puṇyānumodanā*) as follows: "I rejoice with the unsurpassed rejoicing in all the accumulations of merit and wisdom belonging to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three times, to all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and to all sentient beings—those which purify the realm of beings and protect the realm of beings, whether mundane or supramundane—just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know them.
Then: Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the Protector;
homage to the great Saṅgha; constant homage to these three. (51)
The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds. I rejoice in the merit of the world and set my mind upon the awakening of a Buddha. (52)
Until enlightenment, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Supreme Assembly;
I generate the mind of awakening for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of myself and others. (53)
I generate the supreme mind of awakening;
I invite all sentient beings;
I shall practice the desired, excellent conduct of awakening.
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world. ||54||
Thus one should recite the Three Refuges verse. Then, one should offer praise:
He who has himself awakened to Buddhahood—peaceful, without beginning, middle, or end—and having realized it, taught the firm and fearless path for the sake of awakening those who are ignorant.

Homage to him who wields the sword and vajra of wisdom and compassion, the sole cutter of the sprouts of suffering, and the shatterer of the walls of doubt concealed within the thicket of various views. ||55||

Then, one should recite eight times this Queen of Vidyās, which offers an unerring hymn of praise to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: *Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāṃ sarvatra saṃkusumitābhijñārāśini namo 'stu te svāhā*.

Devotion to the Buddha, an inherently guileless nature, loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, practice in renunciation, freedom from attachment to fruits, and association with Bodhisattvas—[these are the qualities].
May my wisdom be sharp, may my birth be in a most noble family, may my body be lovely, and may I possess the eloquence of a Sugata in birth after birth—enough with further elaboration! (56)
A man born of a long-lived family, possessed of keen intellect and learning, with unimpaired faculties, devoted to you, happy, compassionate, gracious, and a true poet; one who honors his mother,
is ever devoted to his father, remembers his past lives, and is endowed with virtuous conduct.
Virtuous in nature, wealthy, devoted to giving, and endowed with spiritual friends. ||57||

O Blessed One, until I attain the state of a Buddha for the sake of the welfare and prosperity of the world— being energetic, strong, beloved, highly esteemed, free from all diseases, compassionate toward sentient beings, retentive of what I have heard, pure in intention, and possessed of purity— [I shall remain].
May I always remain adorned with all these very qualities. ||58||
Having thus made this aspiration, one should recite this hundred-syllable king of mantras, which possesses great merit, is the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas, and is empowered by all Buddhas:

*Namastraiyadhvikānāṃ tathāgatānāṃ sarvatrāpratihatāvāptidharmatābalinām | Aṃ asamasama-samantato'nantatāvāptiśāsani | Hara 2 smara smaraṇa vigatarāgabuddhadharmate | Sara sara samabalā | Hasa hasa traya traya | Gaganamahāvaralakṣaṇe | Jvala jvalanasāgare svāhā!* Then—
May all those throughout every direction who are afflicted by suffering of body and mind obtain oceans of happiness and joy through my merits. (59)
May the god send rain in due season, and may there be an abundance of crops;
may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous. (60)
Without experiencing the suffering of the lower realms and without the practice of austerities, may the world attain Buddhahood with a single divine body. (61)

Having recited this, one should dedicate the merit with this formula for the rejoicing in and dedication of the perfection of wisdom: "Just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones know and see that root of virtue with their Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-eye—its kind, its category, its nature, its essence, its characteristics, and the reality (dharmatā) by which it exists—in that same way do I rejoice in that root of virtue. And just as those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones authorize that root of virtue being dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect awakening, in that same way do I dedicate it."

Thereafter, reciting "Oṃ, I bow with the graceful salutations of all the Tathāgatas to the Blessed One, [the Lord] named so-and-so," or "Jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ! O Lord, accept this handful of flowers, hoḥ!", one should prostrate. Then:
"You have accomplished the welfare of all sentient beings; you have bestowed the accomplishments according to their needs. Go to the realm of the Buddhas, and may you return again. (62)

One should dismiss [the deities] with “Oṃ muḥ svāhā. Thereafter, one should erase the lines of the maṇḍala. Furthermore, the praise of worship has been declared by the Blessed One in the *Śraddhābalādhānamudrāsūtra*: “Mañjuśrī, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to offer daily food of a hundred flavors and divine garments to as many Pratyekabuddhas as there are atoms in all the world-systems. [...]”

"In this way, one might give for as many eons as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges rivers. Yet, Mañjuśrī, another son of noble family or daughter of noble family who should behold a Buddha—whether depicted in a painting or fashioned from a book—generates incalculably more merit than that. How much more so for one who should join their palms in reverence, or offer a flower, or incense, or a lamp! This very person generates incalculably more merit than the former. And in the *Śrī-samāja*:
"One should always worship the Buddhas with the five strands of sensory pleasure according to the ritual procedure."
"Through the fivefold offerings of worship, one may swiftly attain Buddhahood.

(63) "And whoever should worship [the Buddha] while he is still present, and whoever [worships him] after he has passed into parinirvāṇa—if their clarity of mind is equal, there is no distinction in their merit. (64)

By this much, the practice of the counteragent has been explained, as well as the application of the counteragent. Having committed an unwholesome deed, one applies oneself with extreme diligence to a wholesome deed. Or else, as before, in the center of the completed maṇḍala, one should resolve that one’s own chosen deity—such as Lokeśvara and others—is born from its respective seed-syllable; that it is of the single flavor of bodhicitta, which is non-dual with emptiness and compassion; and that it has the nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas by virtue of being of the single flavor of suchness. Having invoked [the deity] as before and placed the Lord of the Family, such as Amitābha, upon its crown, one should observe all the deities in their respective places according to the instruction and perform the worship, praise, mantra-recitation, propitiation, and so forth, as previously described.
And at the conclusion:

*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ sarvavit pūra 2 sūra 2 āvarttābhaye svāhā*. By the mere act of recollecting this once, one has performed worship and service to all the Tathāgatas and prostrated with the head at their feet. Even if one has not performed any worship of the Triple Gem in thought during constant recitation, one should repeat this dhāraṇī. Thus ends the ritual procedure for worshipping the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and others.

The ritual procedure for worship for the purpose of reciting the *Saddharma* is written here according to the oral instructions. First, the practitioner of mantras (mantrī), having performed the washing of hands and feet and so forth, sits upon a comfortable seat. Taking fragrant substances and the like together with water, he consecrates the ground with the mantra: *oṃ vajrasattva vidhnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ*. Having drawn a circular maṇḍala, he consecrates it with the mantra: *oṃ vajrarekhe hūṃ*, and after placing a single flower upon the maṇḍala, he should wash his hands.

Then, in the center of the mandala, one should meditate upon Mount Sumeru, which is adorned with a golden staff at its base and embellished by eight peaks at its summit; it is composed of the jewels of the earth, being constructed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold on its eastern, southern, western, and northern sides. Then, one should meditate upon Pūrvavideha in the shape of a half-moon in front of Sumeru, Jambūdvīpa as a triangle to the south, Aparagodānīya as a circle to the west, and Uttarakuru as a square to the north.

Then, one should meditate upon each of these as being completely filled with ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, diamond, pearl, and coral. Then, having removed the flower previously offered, one should offer a flower upon the mandala while consecrating it with the mantra: *oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ*. One should likewise offer incense and the other offerings as appropriate with the mantras beginning with *oṃ vajradhūpe hūṃ*. Then, having resolved that this entire ritual of worship is the True Dharma (*saddharma*), whose nature is the *dharmakāya* of all the Tathāgatas, and having dedicated it to him, one should place the book of the True Dharma in the center of the mandala, recite it according to the rules, and dedicate all these roots of merit toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Oṃ! The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you, and success has been granted according to your needs.
Go now to the realm of the Buddhas, and may you return once more. (65)

One should dismiss [the deities] with the syllable *muḥ*. This is also stated in the *Bṛhadādibuddhatantra*, because placing yantras and the like upon one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) is prohibited. In that very same [tantra], the maṇḍala for reciting the True Dharma (*saddharmapāṭha*) is described:
"In the east is Pūrvavideha, Jambūdvīpa in the south, Aparagodānīya in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north. (66)
Having worshipped Sumeru in the center, one should worship the subcontinents in the corners with the previously mentioned mantras; situated above those are the Prajñāpāramitā and the others.
One should recite the sublime Dharma with devotion, maintaining one's commitment without interruption;
having performed worship and other services toward it, one should practice everything correctly. (68) Thus it is said.
The Ritual Procedure for Making Offerings through the Recitation of the Sublime Dharma.

Now, the procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhi*) for the purpose of propitiating the deity is described. Here, having performed the purification of the ground and so forth as before, one should meditate on Mount Sumeru in the center of the mandala, and likewise on the four continents in the directions starting from the east. Nearby, one should contemplate the eight sub-continents (*upadvīpa*) known as Deha, Videha, Śāṭhottara-mantrin, Amara-vara, Kuru, and Kaurava, all filled with the seven precious gems. [Then] the mandala—

At the conclusion [of the practice], one should visualize women, men, wheels, jewels, swords, elephants, horses, precious gems, and great treasures in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions. Then, having offered everything to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—or to one’s own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā)—one should resolve that it consists of all the Tathāgatas by virtue of being of one flavor with the bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion, and of one flavor with the higher mind (*adhicitta*). Having dedicated this to them and performed recitations of praise and so forth, one should dedicate the merit as before and then dismiss [the deities]. This is the ritual procedure for propitiating and making offerings to the deity.

For the purpose of accumulating the provisions of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*), one should construct a square mandala during the ritual of worship (*pūjāvidhi*). In this regard, the purification of the ground and the placement of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and so forth should be performed according to the respective *tantra*. Furthermore, the ritual of worship before the Guru, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas should be performed in this manner: having manifested a circular mandala, one should offer a flower in the center with the mantra: *oṃ haḥ mahāmerave namaḥ*. In the eastern direction: *oṃ yaṃ pūrvavidehāya namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ raṃ jambūdvīpāya namaḥ*. In the west: *oṃ laṃ aparagodānīyāya namaḥ*. In the north: *oṃ vaṃ uttarakurave namaḥ*. In the southeast (*āgneyakoṇa*): *oṃ yaḥ upadvīpāya namaḥ*. In the southwest (*nairṛtakoṇa*): *oṃ raḥ upadvīpāya namaḥ*. In the northwest (*vāyavyakoṇa*): *oṃ laḥ upadvīpāya namaḥ*. In the northeast (*aiśānakoṇa*): *oṃ vaḥ upadvīpāya namaḥ*. Again, in the center and the east: *oṃ ya gajaratnāya namaḥ*. In the south: *oṃ ra puruṣaratnāya namaḥ*. In the west: *oṃ la vājiratnāya namaḥ*. In the north: *oṃ va strīratnāya namaḥ*. In the southeast: *oṃ yā khaḍgaratnāya namaḥ*. In the southwest: *oṃ rā cakraratnāya namaḥ*. In the northwest: *oṃ lā maṇiratnāya namaḥ*. In the northeast: *oṃ vā mahānidhānāya namaḥ*.

Having visualized all these as being produced from their respective seeds and possessing their own individual natures, and having worshipped them—seeing the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas atop Mount Sumeru—one should offer them [the merit] and pay homage preceded by the offering of a handful of flowers: *Oṃ āḥ, homage to the glorious Vajra-Guru, the lotus that removes obscurations, who illuminates with perfect gnosis; hūṃ*.
By the rays of whose grace, the darkness is dispelled by the surrounding luster of the jewel of the true nature of the self as it flashes forth,
those with unclouded vision behold their own splendor most exalted.
To that Sun-like Guru, this salutation is offered. ||69||
Thus one should perform the praise of the Guru. This concludes the ritual procedure for the worship of the Guru, the Buddha, and so forth.

The ritual procedure for worship has already been explained for the purpose of attending upon the guru and reciting the sublime Dharma; now it is stated according to a different tradition. One should perform the ritual of worship by means of the previously mentioned mantras of Sumeru and the four continents in the center of the circular maṇḍala and in the directions starting from the east.

One should [place it] below with the *Meru* mantra in the previously mentioned location. In this way, one should dedicate the fruit of the worship to the Preceptor (*ācārya*). And even if external objects are absent, that which is produced from the wish-fulfilling tree of one’s own resolve and offered with a sense of devotion—however slight—leads to exceedingly great fruit for the Guru. This is because all phenomena are preceded by the mind. Furthermore, the Sages have said: "There is no fruit whatsoever for one who offers a collection of objects brought before him while his mind is distracted or dull. For instance: "All recitations and austerities, even if performed over a long period of time..."
"The All-Knowing One has said that [an offering] made with a distracted or dull mind is indeed in vain" (70).

Thus, regarding a communal meal for the Saṅgha, the offering of a gift for the monastery, and even the offering of a gift for the Dharma, both the Dharma and the Saṅgha are to be honored and established by making Mount Meru the presiding object.
Whatever constitutes the livelihood of each individual, one should acquire that through pure means of livelihood.
One should think only of medicine for the sake of pacifying hunger, thirst, and disease. ||71||

As it is said in the *Ugradattaparipṛcchā*: "In this world, O Householder, a householder bodhisattva seeks wealth through righteous means and not through unrighteous means; he seeks it with impartiality and not with partiality; his livelihood is right and not wrong. Then, as [stated]:
"One should offer a bali-oblation and a food offering (naivedya) among the gathered foods, and the foremost portion of alms-food to Hārītī."
The fifth [gift] is always relinquished for the sake of enjoying great fruits. //72//
Therein, one should offer the *sārvabhautika* bali with: *Oṃ akāro mukhaṃ sarvadharmāṇām ādyanutpannatvāt oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

One should offer the food offering (*naivedya*) with: *Oṃ āḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyo vajranaivedye hūṃ*. One should offer two balls of rice to Hārītī with: *Oṃ hārītyai mahāvajrayakṣiṇyai hara hara sarvapāpāni kṣīṃ svāhā*.
"Oṃ, svāhā to those who eat the first portion of the rice-ball!"—thus is the offering of the first portion of the rice-ball.

With the mantra "Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Oṃ, I bestow strength, O garland of splendor! Svāhā," and with "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," one should consecrate the food eight times. Having first touched it with the ring finger and the thumb, one should eat; thus, defects such as poison and the like are pacified.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor noisily, nor with the mouth wide open;
food that is wholesome and moderate in quantity is beneficial, but neither when eaten too slowly nor too hurriedly. (73)

Thereafter, one should offer the discarded morsel with the words, "Svāhā to those who eat the discarded morsel. Having abandoned the remainder without any further intention and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), the Bodhisattva dwelling in the midst of the household should dedicate the merit to all beings residing in every world-system. Whether he has departed from the household life as a renunciant or remains at home, he should proclaim the excellence of his virtuous giving for the sake of satisfying the mind;
and for the sake of protecting the accumulation of merit, he should recite verses on generosity. ||74||
May the king, the lord of donors, and all other multitudes of sentient beings always attain happiness, long life, health, and prosperity. (75)
Through generosity, living beings are brought under one's influence;
through generosity, even enmities come to an end;
and through generosity, even a stranger attains the status of a kinsman.
Therefore, they proclaim that giving is the foremost. 76.
Generosity is an ornament in the world; generosity is the warding off of miserable rebirths.
Generosity is the staircase to heaven; generosity is auspicious and brings peace. (77)
May this gift flourish for the sake of attaining those inexhaustible enjoyments of the Bodhisattvas, which are like the sky. (78)
Thus, these verses on giving are to be recited repeatedly. Furthermore, one should not perform acts such as devotion toward other religious systems.
As it is stated in the *Triśaraṇasaptati*:
"The Three Refuges are protected by the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*)."
One should not perform acts of devotion, worship, or salutation toward other religious systems. ||79||
And in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*: "One should not think that flowers, incense, or lamps are to be given to other deities."

Then, [one should recite]: *Namo samantaprabharājāya tathāgatāyārhate samyaksaṃbuddhāya*. *Namo mañjuśriye kumārabhūtāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya*. Tadyathā—*Oṃ nirālambe nirābhāse jaye jayalabdhe mahāmate dakṣe dakṣiṇāṃ pariśodhaya svāhā*. Whoever shall recite this dhāraṇī even once will purify alms-food even as large as Mount Sumeru; thus one should repeat this "dhāraṇī for the purification of alms-food. Having first performed the vigil of the early night through the study of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), meditation, recitation, and so forth, when going to sleep, one should prostrate with all limbs upon the bed for the purpose of paying homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. And one should make this petition: "May all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas empower me! May they grant me the boon of supreme accomplishment and destroy all calamities! In the latter part of the night, one should again perform everything in the same manner, without confusion and with uninterrupted commitment. For a son of good family or a daughter of good family who acts in this way every day, awakening is not far off. As it has been said:
One should always practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and the other perfections;
in no long time at all, supreme enlightenment will be attained. ||80||
Through the accumulation of the equipment for merit that has arisen from my constant performance of virtuous deeds, may all prosperity be born for the world. (81)
The introduction to the beginner's practice is completed.
Human birth is difficult to obtain in this world; the arising of a Buddha is exceedingly difficult to obtain; even more difficult than that is faith, renunciation, and spiritual practice.

"With a firm mind set on awakening out of compassion for all sentient beings, and for the sake of pacifying all suffering—this is the succession of those things most difficult to obtain. Thus [ends the work].
The length of this text is one hundred [stanzas]. (5)
This is the work of the venerable scholar and elder Mañjukīrti.
